content: The development of prosthetic and orthotic technologies has been largely influenced by market demand rather than actual need. While significant advancements have been made in these technologies, the focus has predominantly been on high-income settings. In contrast, there has been limited research and development tailored to the needs of lowand middle-income countries, where financial incentives for such innovations are minimal or nonexistent. However, the large potential market in these regions should serve as a motivation for suppliers to invest in affordable solutions. Some commercial enterprises have attempted to create basic prosthetic and orthotic products, and international organizations have developed cost-effective technologies that are now widely used in lowand middle-income countries. Additionally, certain service providers in these regions manufacture affordable components. Despite these efforts, there remains a significant global need for alternative, low-cost designs that can dramatically increase accessibility for individuals in poorer settings. Such innovations could also create new business opportunities through the mass production of high-quality, cost-effective components. As seen in the pharmaceutical industry, assistive products can be made affordable with the collaboration of various stakeholders. This would require the involvement of prosthetics and orthotics experts, private entrepreneurs, governments, service providers, user representatives, international organizations, funding agencies, and investors. Prosthetics and orthotics personnel are categorized into three main groups: prosthetists and orthotists, associate prosthetists and orthotists, and prosthetics and orthotics technicians. Prosthetists and orthotists, along with their associates, are collectively referred to as clinicians, as they primarily perform clinical work. Technicians and other support personnel are considered non-clinicians. Prosthetists and orthotists are healthcare professionals responsible for the overall management of prosthetic and orthotic treatments. They are trained to assess user needs, prescribe treatments, determine technical specifications, take measurements and images, prepare models for device manufacturing, fit devices, and evaluate treatment outcomes. They must have a comprehensive understanding of the fabrication process to guide and supervise technicians and support staff. Their training equips them with broad clinical competencies, and they are encouraged to gain further expertise, assume leadership roles, and engage in research and evidence-based practice. Many pursue advanced education at the master's or doctoral level. Associate prosthetists and orthotists perform similar clinical tasks but with more limited competencies. They conduct less research and are less involved in advancing service delivery methods. They work under the supervision of prosthetists or orthotists and have a delegated scope of practice. Like their senior counterparts, associates supervise non-clinicians and must understand all technical aspects of the work. Prosthetics and orthotics technicians are responsible for fabricating prostheses and orthoses based on technical specifications provided by clinicians. They process materials, assemble components, prepare products for fitting, and finalize them for delivery. Technicians are knowledgeable about materials, technical processes, and safe practices. Under controlled circumstances, they may assist clinicians in certain clinical tasks to improve service accessibility, provided they have acquired the necessary skills and work under close supervision. Support personnel include workers without formal training in prosthetics or orthotics who perform essential non-clinical tasks, such as plastic-forming or plaster work. Other support roles include storekeepers, cleaners, and maintenance workers. Administrative personnel, such as receptionists, play a crucial role in user interactions and ensuring user-centered services. Their communication skills and ability to build positive relationships with users can significantly influence rehabilitation outcomes. Training administrative staff and involving long-term service users in administrative roles can enhance service quality and provide peer support. Medical specialists are integral to prosthetics and orthotics services, particularly in multidisciplinary rehabilitation teams. These specialists include physicians in physical and rehabilitation medicine, amputation surgery, orthopedics, vascular surgery, neurology, rheumatology, pediatrics, geriatrics, and other relevant fields. Physiotherapists and occupational therapists are also critical to successful service delivery, especially those specializing in areas such as amputation rehabilitation, stroke, cerebral palsy, and spinal conditions. Other allied health professionals, such as podiatrists, psychologists, and biomedical engineers, contribute to the effectiveness of prosthetics and orthotics services. In complex cases, prosthetics and orthotics services should be delivered by multidisciplinary rehabilitation teams with shared goals and a unified team identity. These teams assess user needs, develop holistic treatment plans, and evaluate outcomes. Team members may include prosthetists, orthotists, physicians, physiotherapists, occupational therapists, nurses, psychologists, and social workers. Users and their families should also be considered part of the team and involved in decision-making. In resource-limited settings, the team may consist of just the user and one rehabilitation professional. Teamwork allows for task-sharing and learning among members, which can alleviate service pressures and improve cost-effectiveness. Training for prosthetics and orthotics personnel must be significantly expanded to ensure equitable access to services. Training programs should be integrated into national health education systems and offered alongside courses for other rehabilitation professionals. Education combines theoretical and practical training in health sciences and engineering. Students typically begin with classroom-based learning, followed by supervised clinical practice in controlled environments. This approach helps develop skills in assessment, fitting, and alignment using evidence-based techniques. Practical skills are further honed through supervised placements. Technician training focuses on product preparation and the use of various materials, tools, and machines. Training pathways should allow for progression to higher levels, enabling technicians to advance to clinical roles and associates to become prosthetists and orthotists. Modular courses and blended learning approaches, which combine online theory with hands-on practice, are effective and allow participants to continue working while training. These methods are particularly useful in emergency contexts and regions with limited training opportunities.
